shapes.name: Text 42
shapes.text: 7 modules · quiz + scenario in each · capstone hand · precedes the single-file HTML build

slides.notes: Hey, welcome in. So you want to play American mahjong — with friends, or maybe you're brave enough to sit down with total strangers. Good news: it's absolutely learnable, and by the end of this course you'll play a full hand without a rulebook open on your knee. Everything here follows standard American play — the common rules you'll meet at most tables — and one number to hold onto from the start: you keep thirteen tiles in your hand, and the dealer, East, holds fourteen. Let's get you table-ready.

shapes.name: Text 46
shapes.text: Rules basis: standard American (NMJL-style) play — updated from the booklet where the two differ.

slides.notes: Here's the road ahead. Seven modules, each one short: you'll listen to a quick lesson, take a concept check, then apply what you learned to a real game situation. Module one is all about the tiles themselves, because nothing else works until you can name what's in your hand. Then we set the table, learn the goal, run the Charleston, play real turns, score a win, and finish with the habits that make you welcome at any table. At the very end, a capstone: one complete hand, played start to finish.

shapes.name: Text 36
shapes.text: The tell: if you hear “chow,” “run,” or “fu and fan,” you’re at a Chinese table — politely confirm before sitting down.

slides.notes: One quick guardrail before we start. There's more than one mahjong in the world. Chinese mahjong builds free-form hands out of runs and uses a points-and-doubles system called fu and fan. American mahjong — our game — is different: you match one specific hand printed on a card, there are no runs at all, and it adds jokers, flowers, and a pre-game tile swap called the Charleston. So here's the tell: if you ever hear someone say "chow," "run," or "fu and fan," you're at a Chinese table. Different game. Politely check before you sit down.

shapes.name: Text 5
shapes.text: The full set: 152 tiles in play

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: 1–9, four of each — the 1 Bam is a bird

shapes.name: Text 21
shapes.text: North, East, West, South — four of each

shapes.name: Text 25
shapes.text: Red, Green, White (“Soap”) — four of each

shapes.name: Text 87
shapes.text: Any extra tiles in the box are spares — set them aside.

shapes.name: Text 88
shapes.text: Learners must ID every tile on sight before Module 2 — the next four screens drill each family.

slides.notes: Let's open the box. American mahjong plays with one hundred fifty-two tiles, and they sort into seven families. Thirty-six Dots, thirty-six Bams, thirty-six Craks — those are your three suits, numbers one through nine, four copies of each. Then sixteen Winds — north, east, west, south, four of each. Twelve Dragons — red, green, and white, four of each. Eight Flowers. And eight Jokers, the wild tiles that make American mahjong American. Thirty-six, thirty-six, thirty-six, sixteen, twelve, eight, and eight — one fifty-two. Anything else in the box is a spare. Over the next few minutes we'll walk each family so every tile reads instantly.

shapes.name: Text 169
shapes.text:
Each Dot tile shows its number as a pattern of circles; the small corner number is your fast read.
Four copies of each tile — 36 Dots in the set. Colors vary by set; the patterns don’t.

shapes.name: Text 172
shapes.text: The 1 Dot is the big single medallion — beginners sometimes mistake it for a flower. If it’s one large circle, it’s the 1 Dot.

slides.notes: First suit: the Dots, sometimes called Circles. Each Dot tile shows its number as a pattern of circles — one circle for the one, two for the two, all the way up to a three-by-three grid for the nine. And there's a shortcut printed right on the tile: a small number in the corner. Trust the corner. One thing to watch: the one Dot is a single big medallion, and brand-new players sometimes mistake it for a flower. If it's one large circle, it's the one Dot. Four copies of every number — thirty-six Dots in all.

shapes.name: Text 129
shapes.text: ★  THE ONE EVERYONE MISSES: the 1 Bam is a BIRD

shapes.name: Text 130
shapes.text: There are no bamboo sticks on the 1 Bam — it’s a bird on a perch. New players discard it thinking it’s a bonus tile, or fail to call it. Drill it until the bird instantly reads as “1 Bam.”

shapes.name: Text 132
shapes.text: 2–9 show that many bamboo sticks; corner number confirms. Four of each — 36 Bams total.

slides.notes: Second suit: the Bams, short for bamboo. Twos through nines show that many bamboo sticks — count the sticks or read the corner number. But here's the one everybody misses, so lean in: the one Bam is a bird. No sticks at all — a bird sitting on a perch. New players throw it away thinking it's a decoration, or stare right past it when they need it. Burn this in now: bird equals one Bam. Four of each, thirty-six total.

shapes.name: Text 53
shapes.text:
Top character = the number (一 through 九). Bottom red character 萬 (“wan,” ten-thousand) marks the suit.
You never need to read Chinese: the Arabic numeral in the corner tells you the number on American sets.

shapes.name: Text 55
shapes.text: Four of each — 36 Craks total. If the tile has the red 萬 at the bottom, it’s a Crak; say the corner number and “Crak.”

slides.notes: Third suit: the Craks, short for characters. Each Crak has two Chinese characters: the top one is the number, and the bottom one — the red character, wan — is the suit marker. Here's the good news: you never need to read Chinese. American sets print the number in the corner, so your read is simply: red character at the bottom means Crak, corner number tells you which one. "Five Crak." Done. Four of each, thirty-six total.

shapes.name: Text 24
shapes.text: The corner letter (N·E·W·S) is your read — no Chinese needed. Winds appear in many card hands, including NEWS runs.

shapes.name: Text 36
shapes.text: The Soap is just a bone tile with a blue frame — it looks blank. It is NOT a spare: it’s the White dragon, and on the card it also stands in as zero (0).

shapes.name: Text 39
shapes.text: When a card hand mixes a suit with dragons: Craks go with Red · Bams go with Green · Dots go with Soap (White). Memory hook: C-R, B-G, D-W.

slides.notes: Now the honor tiles. Winds first: north, east, west, and south, and every wind has its letter printed in the corner — N, E, W, S — so they read at a glance. Four of each, sixteen winds. Then the Dragons, three colors: the red dragon, the green dragon, and the white dragon. The white one deserves special attention — it's basically a blank tile with a blue frame, and players call it the Soap. It is not a spare! It's a live dragon, and on the card it can even stand in for the number zero. Last thing, and it matters for reading the card: when a hand mixes a suit with dragons, they pair up — Craks with red, Bams with green, Dots with the Soap. C-R, B-G, D-W.

shapes.name: Text 27
shapes.text:
All 8 flowers are interchangeable — any flower fills any “F” on the card, whatever its number or picture.
Flowers are real hand tiles in American play, not bonuses: many card hands require them.
Seasons count as flowers in American sets — that’s why there are 8.

shapes.name: Text 35
shapes.text: Matches your set: red JOKER, green dragon face in a blue ring.

shapes.name: Text 37
shapes.text: Joker quick rules (full rules in Module 3)

shapes.name: Text 38
shapes.text:
Wild — but only inside groups of 3+ (pung, kong, quint)
Never in a pair, never as a single, never in NEWS-style runs of singles
Never passed in the Charleston
Unique to American mahjong

slides.notes: Two special families left. Flowers: there are eight, numbered one through eight, and here's the American twist — they're all interchangeable. Any flower fills any flower spot in a hand, no matter its number or picture. And flowers are real working tiles here, not bonuses; plenty of winning hands require them. Then the stars of the show: eight Jokers, wild tiles unique to American mahjong. A joker can stand in for other tiles — but under strict rules we'll cover properly in module three. The headline version: jokers work only inside groups of three or more. Never in a pair, never alone, and never, ever passed in the Charleston.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text: 1.  Which suit’s “1” tile is a bird?

shapes.text: 2.  What tile is nicknamed the “Soap,” and what else can it do?

shapes.text: ✓  The White dragon (blank with a blue frame). On the card it can also serve as zero.

shapes.name: Text 12
shapes.text: 3.  How many tiles are in play, and how many are jokers?

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: You draw a bone-colored tile with nothing on it but a blue rectangular frame. A tablemate says “spare tile, toss it.” What is it really?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: It’s the Soap — the White dragon. It’s a live, playable tile (and the card’s zero). Keep or discard it on strategy, not because it looks blank.

slides.notes: Time for your first check. Pause on each question, answer out loud, then compare. And try the scenario before you reveal it — it's the blank-looking tile that fools everyone at least once.

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: Highest roll deals and holds the extra tile. East rotates right after each hand.

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: All 152 tiles face down. Each player: 19 stacks long, 2 tiles high (38 tiles).

shapes.name: Text 17
shapes.text: East rolls, counts that many stacks from the right of a wall, and deals from there: 4 tiles at a time until everyone has 12, then 1 more each — East takes 2.

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: Everyone 13 tiles · East 14 · play moves counter-clockwise (to your right)

slides.notes: Let's set the table. Step one: everybody rolls the dice, and the highest roll becomes East — the dealer. East gets the extra tile and, after each hand, the deal rotates to the right. Step two: build the wall. All one fifty-two tiles go face down, and each player builds a wall in front of their rack — nineteen stacks long, two tiles high. Four walls, one square, every tile accounted for. Step three: East rolls again, counts that many stacks in from the right of the indicated wall, and the deal begins there — four tiles at a time around the table until everyone has twelve, then one more each, with East taking two. Final count, say it with me: everyone thirteen, East fourteen. And play will move counter-clockwise — to the right.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text: 1.  How big is each player’s wall?

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: ✓  19 stacks long, 2 tiles high — 38 tiles; four walls hold all 152.

shapes.name: Text 10
shapes.text: 2.  After the deal, who holds 14 tiles?

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: ✓  Only East. Everyone else holds 13. East opens by discarding one.

shapes.name: Text 12
shapes.text: 3.  Which direction does the turn move?

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: ✓  Counter-clockwise — to the right of the player who just went.

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: East rolls the dice and gets 7. What does East do with that number?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: Count 7 stacks in from the right-hand end of the indicated wall and break there — dealing starts from that point, 4 tiles at a time.

slides.notes: Quick check on the setup. If you can answer these three cold, you can physically start a game anywhere. The scenario walks the dice roll — the piece most beginners have to see once before it clicks.

shapes.name: Text 5
shapes.text: The card, and the sets that build it

shapes.name: Text 7
shapes.text: You win by matching the card

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text:
Every legal hand is printed on the players’ card (most tables use the NMJL card, reissued every year).
Your 14 tiles must match one listed hand exactly — no freestyle combinations.
Hands are worth 25–75 points, printed beside each hand.

shapes.name: Text 75
shapes.text: five identical — only possible with jokers

shapes.name: Text 78
shapes.text:
Call a discard to complete a pung/kong/quint → that set is exposed face-up on your rack.
Hands marked C (concealed) on the card allow no exposures — you may only claim a discard for mahjong itself.
Exposed hands are easier; concealed hands score more.

shapes.name: Text 80
shapes.text: A “sextet” (6) appears on some cards — same idea, jokers required. Your table’s card governs.

slides.notes: So what are you actually building? Here's the heart of American mahjong: you win by matching your fourteen tiles, exactly, to one of the hands printed on the card — most tables use the National Mah Jongg League card, which is reissued every year. No freestyle. Your building blocks are simple: a pair is two identical tiles, a pung is three, a kong is four, and a quint is five — and since only four copies of any tile exist, a quint is only possible with jokers. One more distinction that shapes your whole game: exposed versus concealed. When you call a discard to finish a pung, kong, or quint, that set gets flipped face-up on your rack — exposed. Hands marked C on the card are concealed: no exposures allowed, and you can only claim a discard for the win itself. Concealed is harder, and it pays more.

shapes.name: Text 5
shapes.text: Joker rules — strict, and worth memorizing

shapes.name: Text 63
shapes.text: Kong of 7 Bams using a joker — jokers fill any spot in a group of 3 or more (pung, kong, quint, sextet).

shapes.name: Text 84
shapes.text: No joker in a pair. No joker as a single (including year, NEWS, or 2026-style number hands). This is the #1 joker error.

shapes.name: Text 87
shapes.text:
On your turn (after drawing), if any player’s exposed set contains a joker and you hold the matching natural tile, you may swap your tile for that joker — including from your own exposures.
A discarded joker is just a dead discard: no one may call it, and it stops being wild.
Jokers are never passed in the Charleston — receive one by mistake and it goes straight back.

slides.notes: Joker rules — strict, short, and worth memorizing, because joker mistakes are the most common fouls in the game. Rule one: jokers live only in groups of three or more. A pung, a kong, a quint — perfect. A pair? Never. A single tile? Never. Rule two — and this one wins games — the joker exchange. On your turn, after you draw, if any exposed set on the table shows a joker and you're holding the matching real tile, you can swap your tile for that joker. Even from your own exposures. A free wild tile, just for paying attention. Rule three: a discarded joker is dead — nobody can call it, and its wildness is gone. And rule four: jokers never travel in the Charleston. If someone passes you one by mistake, straight back it goes.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text: 1.  Can a joker complete a pair?

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: ✓  No. Jokers work only in groups of 3+ — pung, kong, quint, sextet.

shapes.name: Text 10
shapes.text: 2.  What is a quint, and why does it need jokers?

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: ✓  Five identical tiles; only four naturals exist, so at least one joker is required.

shapes.name: Text 12
shapes.text: 3.  Your hand is marked C on the card. When may you call a discard?

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: ✓  Only for mahjong itself — concealed hands allow no exposures.

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: An opponent’s exposed kong of 4 Craks shows a joker, and you’re holding a natural 4 Crak you don’t need there. What’s your move?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: On your turn, after you draw: exchange your natural 4 Crak for their joker. You now own a wild tile — one of the strongest moves in the game.

slides.notes: Check yourself on the card and the jokers. The scenario is the joker exchange — honestly one of the most satisfying moves in the game, and one many beginners never realize they're allowed to make.

shapes.name: Text 42
shapes.text: 3 tiles per pass · any single player may stop the second Charleston before it starts

shapes.name: Text 45
shapes.text: only on the LAST pass of each Charleston — pass received tiles unseen

shapes.name: Text 47
shapes.text: after it all ends: swap 0–3 with the player across; the lower number rules

shapes.name: Text 49
shapes.text: never passed — hand one back immediately if you receive it

slides.notes: Now the famous part: the Charleston, the pre-game tile swap. First Charleston — this one's required: pass three tiles to your right, then three across the table, then three to your left. Right, across, left. Second Charleston — optional, and here's the key: it takes everyone. Any single player can call it off. If it runs, it mirrors back: left, across, right. Two special moves. The blind pass: on the last pass of either Charleston, if you love your hand, you may pass along tiles you just received without even looking at them. And the courtesy pass: after all the passing ends, you and the player across from you may swap zero to three tiles — and the lower number rules. You want three, they want one? You each pass one. And the golden rule one more time: jokers never pass.

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: ✓  Right, across, left — three tiles each pass.

shapes.name: Text 10
shapes.text: 2.  When is a blind pass allowed?

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: ✓  Only on the last pass of each Charleston (first’s left; second’s right).

shapes.name: Text 12
shapes.text: 3.  Courtesy pass: you want to swap 3, the player across wants 1.

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: ✓  You each pass 1 — the lower number always governs.

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: The table finishes the first Charleston. Three players want the second; one says no. What happens?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: No second Charleston — any single player can stop it. The table moves straight to the optional courtesy pass, then East discards to start play.

slides.notes: Charleston check. The pass order, the blind pass timing, and the courtesy-pass numbers game are the three things that trip up new players — nail these and you'll look like a veteran before the first tile is ever drawn.

shapes.name: Text 25
shapes.text:
Only the most recent discard is callable — earlier ones are gone.
Call to expose a pung, kong, or quint — or to declare mahjong.
A pair may only be completed by a discard if it wins the game.
Name the tile correctly; a wrong name voids the claim.
Two callers? Mahjong beats an exposure call; otherwise the player next in turn from the discarder gets it.
After you call, expose the full set on your rack, then discard.

shapes.name: Text 28
shapes.text:
Don’t draw out of turn; look at only one wall tile per draw.
Wrong tile count (not 13/14)? Your hand is DEAD: stop playing, keep tiles hidden, and you still pay the winner.
A false “Mah Jongg” with tiles exposed also kills the hand.
Antidote: one-second count before every discard.

shapes.name: Text 29
shapes.text: Wall empties with no winner → wall game (covered in scoring).

slides.notes: Let's play. On your turn: draw one tile from the wall, rack it, and discard one face-up in the middle — naming it out loud. "Six Dot." "Soap." Then it's the next player's turn, moving counter-clockwise. Simple rhythm, one golden number: after your discard you hold exactly thirteen. Now, calling. Only the most recent discard is ever up for grabs — the moment the next player draws, it's gone. You can call a discard to expose a pung, kong, or quint, or to declare mahjong. A pair? Only if it wins you the game on the spot. If two players want the same tile, mahjong beats an exposure, and otherwise it goes to whoever's turn comes next. And the thing to fear: the dead hand. Wrong tile count — twelve tiles, fifteen tiles — and you're out: you stop playing, keep your tiles hidden, and you still pay the winner. The cure costs one second: count before every discard.

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: ✓  Only the most recent one — once the next player draws, it’s dead.

shapes.name: Text 10
shapes.text: 2.  May you call a discard to finish a pair?

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: ✓  Only if that pair completes your mahjong. Otherwise pairs come from the wall.

shapes.name: Text 12
shapes.text: 3.  Two players call the same tile — who wins?

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: ✓  A mahjong call beats an exposure call; between equals, the player next in turn from the discarder.

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: Mid-game you glance down and count 12 tiles. What now?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: Your hand is dead: announce it, stop drawing and discarding, keep your tiles concealed — and you still pay the winner at the end. This is why the pre-discard count matters.

slides.notes: Turn mechanics check. The scenario is the dead hand — it stings, but walking through it once here means you'll never actually live it at the table.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text:
14th tile completes a card hand → say “Mah Jongg” and show it.
The table verifies against the card.
Its printed value (25–75) is the base.

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: Throwing the winning tile is expensive — defense matters.

shapes.name: Text 17
shapes.text: Draw your own winning tile from the wall and all three opponents pay double.

shapes.name: Text 20
shapes.text:
Jokerless: winning with zero jokers doubles the value again — bonuses stack. (Doesn’t apply to Singles-and-Pairs hands, which can’t use jokers anyway.)
Wall game: tiles run out with no winner → nobody pays; shuffle and redeal.
Values and hands come from the card in play — confirm the year before starting.

shapes.name: Text 23
shapes.text:
25-pt hand, won on a discard:
discarder pays 50 · others pay 25 each = 100 in.
Same hand self-picked & jokerless:
25 × 2 × 2 = 100 from each player.

slides.notes: The good part: getting paid. When your fourteenth tile completes a card hand, say "Mah Jongg," show your tiles, and the table checks them against the card. The printed value — twenty-five to seventy-five points — is your base. Then how you won sets the multiplier. Won on somebody's discard? That player pays you double, and the other two pay single — which is why careless discards are expensive. Drew the winning tile yourself off the wall? Self-pick: everybody pays double. And if your winning hand used zero jokers, double it again — the bonuses stack. Quick example: a twenty-five point hand, self-picked, jokerless — twenty-five, doubled, doubled — that's a hundred from every player. One more outcome to know: if the wall runs out with no winner, that's a wall game. Nobody pays. Shuffle up, rotate East, go again.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text: 1.  A 25-point hand wins on Priya’s discard. Who pays what?

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: ✓  Priya pays 50 (double); the other two pay 25 each.

shapes.name: Text 10
shapes.text: 2.  A 30-point hand wins by self-pick. Who pays what?

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: ✓  All three opponents pay 60 — self-pick doubles for everyone.

shapes.name: Text 12
shapes.text: 3.  What does a jokerless win add?

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: ✓  Another doubling, stacked on top (not applicable to Singles-and-Pairs hands).

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: The last wall tile is drawn and discarded with no winner. What happens to payments?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: It’s a wall game: no one pays anything. Shuffle, rebuild the walls, rotate East to the right, and deal the next hand.

slides.notes: Scoring check. Do the arithmetic out loud on these — payment math is the thing veteran players silently judge, and the thing you'll be glad is automatic.

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: “Are we on this year’s NMJL card?” Hands and values change every year — bring or borrow the right one.

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: Courtesy pass in use? Any local joker or payment quirks? Thirty seconds now prevents every argument later.

shapes.name: Text 21
shapes.text: Chips, coins, or just score? Confirm what a point is worth before anyone owes anything.

shapes.name: Text 24
shapes.text:
Keep pace — draw, decide, discard; the table has a rhythm.
Name every discard clearly; call claims promptly.
Racks hide your hand; comment on no one’s tiles but your own.
Win and lose the same way: pleasantly.

shapes.name: Text 27
shapes.text: Before every discard: Do I have 13? Is this the tile I mean to throw? That glance is the whole difference between a smooth player and a dead hand.

slides.notes: Last module: sitting down with strangers and looking like you belong. Three questions before the first Charleston. One: which card are we on? The card changes every year, and playing last year's hands is the classic newcomer mistake. Two: any house rules? Courtesy pass, payment quirks — thirty seconds now saves an argument later. Three: what are the stakes? Chips, coins, or bragging rights — know before anyone owes anything. Then just be good company: keep the rhythm moving, name your discards clearly, never comment on anyone's tiles, and win or lose the same pleasant way. And keep your one-second self-check: thirteen tiles? Right tile? Discard.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text: 1.  What’s the first question at an unfamiliar table?

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: ✓  Which card (and which year) is in play — it defines every legal hand and value.

shapes.name: Text 10
shapes.text: 2.  You call a discard but name it wrong. What happens?

shapes.text: ✓  The claim is void. Name tiles exactly: “five Bam,” “Soap,” “north.”

shapes.text: 3.  What’s the habit that prevents most beginner errors?

shapes.name: Text 13

shapes.name: Text 16
shapes.text: You join three strangers at a café. In twenty seconds, what do you ask before tiles move?

shapes.name: Text 19
shapes.text: “Which year’s card are we on? Any house rules I should know — courtesy pass, payments? And what are we playing for?” Then build your wall like you’ve done it forever.

slides.notes: Final module check. The scenario is your twenty-second script for joining a strange table — practice saying it out loud once, and that first café game will feel like your hundredth.

shapes.text: Mastery bar:  ≤ 2 procedural errors  ·  0 illegal claims  ·  correct final payout

slides.notes: This is where it all comes together: the capstone. One complete hand, start to finish — live with three other players if you can, or through the guided walkthrough. You'll set up, deal thirteen-fourteen, run the Charleston, play real turns with at least one legal call, handle jokers lawfully, catch a planted trap, and score the win — payments and all. The bar: no more than two procedural slips, zero illegal claims, and the payout computed correctly. Clear that, and you're not learning mahjong anymore. You're playing it.

shapes.name: Text 8
shapes.text: Name any of the 152 tiles on sight — including the 1 Bam bird and the Soap

shapes.name: Text 11
shapes.text: Pair the right dragon with the right suit (Crak-Red, Bam-Green, Dot-Soap)

shapes.name: Text 14
shapes.text: Build a 19×2 wall, roll for East, and deal 13/14 without prompting

shapes.name: Text 17
shapes.text: Run both Charlestons, a blind pass, and a courtesy pass correctly

shapes.name: Text 20
shapes.text: Keep exactly 13 tiles and catch a dead hand — yours or anyone’s

shapes.name: Text 23
shapes.text: Use jokers only in 3+ groups, and spot an available joker exchange

shapes.name: Text 26
shapes.text: Call only the latest discard, name it exactly, expose correctly

shapes.name: Text 29
shapes.text: Score any win: discard double, self-pick double, jokerless stack, wall game

shapes.name: Text 30
shapes.text: All eight, without notes → the learner is table-ready.

slides.notes: Before you go find a game, run this list honestly. Eight skills, no notes allowed. Every one of them maps to a module you've finished, so anything shaky — jump back, it's a two-minute refresh. All eight solid? Then there's nothing left to learn from me that a real table won't teach you better.

shapes.name: Text 1
shapes.text: Approve → I build the single-file HTML course

shapes.name: Text 5
shapes.text: All 7 modules, quizzes, scenarios, capstone & checklist — same text, same order.

shapes.name: Text 9
shapes.text: Every tile you just verified redrawn as inline SVG — crisp at any size, zero external files.

shapes.name: Text 13
shapes.text: Tile-ID flash drills, tap-to-answer quizzes with instant grading, reveal-style scenarios, progress tracking.

shapes.name: Text 17
shapes.text: Self-contained, offline-capable, no folders — open it anywhere.

shapes.name: Text 18
shapes.text: Review this deck for content errors — rules, tile art, wording — and send corrections. The HTML build follows your sign-off.

slides.notes: That's the course. You know all one hundred fifty-two tiles, the setup, the card, the Charleston, real turns, real scoring, and how to sit down anywhere with confidence. Grab your set, find three people, and play a hand tonight. The tiles are waiting. Good luck — and may you always be jokerless when it counts.
